messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: School Counselor
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Stress: Stress, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure, Olfactory (Smell): Related smells
  Maladaptive Strategies: Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time, Avoid Police: Police, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Marcus

Marcus was thirty-two when it happened. He had been working as a school counselor for six years at Lincoln Middle School, a position he took seriously—the kind of man who stayed late to finish case notes, who remembered the names of kids' siblings, who believed that showing up for students mattered. On an April afternoon in 2022, he was driving home from a professional development workshop when a child darted into the street from between two parked cars. Marcus was going thirty-five miles per hour. He braked hard, but the physics of the moment were unforgiving. The boy—he learned later his name was Tyler, age nine—went down beneath the front wheel. The sound was not like anything Marcus had ever heard: a wet, heavy crunch that seemed to separate him from the world as he had known it. He sat in his car for what might have been seconds or minutes, unable to move, unable to breathe properly. When he got out, there was blood on the asphalt and on the undercarriage of his vehicle. Tyler's mother was screaming. The police arrived. An ambulance. The hospital. Tyler survived, but with a fractured femur and internal injuries that required surgery.

Marcus was not charged. The police investigation concluded the accident was unavoidable. But the conclusion did nothing to shift what had crystallized in Marcus's mind in those first hours: that he had done this. That something in how he was—his attention, his reflexes, his choices that day—had been fundamentally wrong. He had come to believe that he could not trust himself to do the right thing, that his judgment was broken in some irreparable way. How could he have been going that fast in a school zone? Why had he not been more alert? The questions spiraled without resolution.

In the weeks that followed, sleep became impossible. Marcus would lie awake beside his wife, Sarah, his body rigid, his mind cycling through the accident frame by frame. He was certain that if he allowed himself to sleep, something catastrophic would happen—to her, to someone else. Staying alert felt like the only responsible thing left to do. He began keeping his mind occupied constantly: podcasts during his commute, audiobooks at night, work emails answered at two in the morning. Anything to prevent the memory from surfacing. But the memory surfaced anyway, and when it did, it was complete and overwhelming. He could smell the metallic tang of blood, feel the slight vibration of impact travel through the steering wheel, hear that sound again, see Tyler's body in the street. It was not a memory—it was the event itself, happening again, indistinguishable from the original moment.

The smell trigger was the worst. One morning at school, a student came to his office after a nosebleed, and the scent of blood hit Marcus before he could process what was happening. His hands shook so violently he could not hold his pen. His heart raced as though he were about to crash again. He excused himself to the bathroom and sat on the floor of a stall for twenty minutes. It was the same with medical procedures: when his wife insisted he get a physical, the smell of the examination room—antiseptic, sterile, carrying some echo of hospitals and trauma—sent him spiraling. He scheduled the appointment but cancelled it twice. His doctor's office stopped calling.

At work, his colleagues began to notice his distance. He stopped attending staff meetings, claiming scheduling conflicts. He avoided the parking lot where his car sat, taking a longer route through the building. More significantly, he found himself unable to counsel students effectively. A girl came to him with anxiety about an accident she had witnessed, and Marcus realized halfway through the session that his own hands were trembling, that he could not speak about trauma without his voice cracking. He requested a transfer to administrative duties. His supervisor, concerned, suggested he take some time off. Marcus refused. Taking time off meant being alone with his thoughts, and his thoughts were a prison.

Now, two years later, Marcus carries the weight of a life he believes has been destroyed. He avoids thinking about the accident through constant distraction, yet the memory intrudes anyway—vivid, sensory, present. He avoids police, crossing the street if he sees a patrol car, terrified that new information will emerge, that he will be blamed retroactively. He avoids the stress of his former role, though the avoidance itself has become a kind of professional death, a slow erosion of the career he once valued. Sarah has grown quiet around him, sensing his shame but unable to reach him. Marcus has not told anyone the full weight of what he carries: the certainty that he is dangerous, that his judgment cannot be trusted, that the life he had—the marriage, the work, the sense of being someone who helped people—has been irrevocably taken from him.

It was Sarah who finally insisted he seek help. She found a therapist's number on his phone's search history, evidence that some part of him was looking for a way out, and she made the appointment for him. Marcus arrived at the first session terrified and ashamed, hoping desperately that someone could tell him how to live with what he had done, while fearing that no one could.
